title: Keeping safe with electricity: sockets, wires and water

summary.text: The electricity in the wall is about 150 times stronger than a torch cell, and it can travel through water and through people. That is why children never touch sockets, plugs or broken wires, and never touch a switch with wet hands. Your child tests how dry their hands really are after shaking, wiping on clothes and using a towel, and sees how far one spilled tumbler of water spreads. They also find out why a crow can sit on a wire, and what to do if something goes wrong.
summary.art: A girl of seven drying her hands on a towel beside a switch board, with a sheet of newspaper on the table showing damp fingerprints.

intro.hook: You can hold a torch cell in your hand and feel nothing. The wall socket also gives electricity. So why must you never touch it?
intro.text: The electricity from a torch cell is weak. The electricity in the wall socket is very strong, strong enough to hurt or kill a person. It can travel through water, and through your body. In this unit you test how much water stays on your hands after you wash them. You see how far a spill can run. And you learn the rules that keep you safe, and the reason for each one.
intro.art: A child's open hand holding a torch cell, next to a wall socket with a red cross drawn beside it.

outcomes: By the end I can say why the electricity in the wall is dangerous, and why a torch cell is safe to hold.
By the end I can say the rules: never touch sockets, plugs or broken wires, and never poke anything into a socket.
By the end I can explain why water and electricity must be kept apart, and show from my test why hands must be towel-dry.
By the end I can say what to do if I see a spark, a broken wire, or someone getting a shock.
By the end I can explain why a bird can sit on a wire, and why kites and ladders must stay far from wires.
By the end I can name things in my home that keep us safe: plastic covers, socket shutters and the main switch.

terms.meaning: Electricity is a kind of energy that flows along wires. It makes fans turn, lights glow and phones charge.
terms.example: When you press the switch, electricity flows to the fan and the fan turns.
terms.art: A ceiling fan turning, with a dotted line running from a switch board along the wall to the fan.

terms.meaning: Mains electricity is the strong electricity that comes into our homes along wires from a power station. It is in every wall socket. It can hurt or kill a person.
terms.example: The fridge, the mixer and the iron all run on mains electricity.
terms.art: Electric wires on poles running from a far-off power station to a block of flats.

terms.meaning: A cell is a small store of weak electricity. Many people call it a battery.
terms.example: A TV remote and a wall clock run on cells.
terms.art: Two round torch cells and a remote with its back open.

terms.meaning: A socket is the place in the wall with holes, where a plug goes in. The holes lead to mains electricity.
terms.example: The socket on the switch board in the kitchen has three holes.
terms.art: A white Indian switch board with two switches and a three-hole socket.

terms.meaning: A plug is the end of a machine's wire. It has metal pins that fit into a socket.
terms.example: The mixer's plug has three metal pins.
terms.art: A three-pin plug with its plastic body and metal pins.

terms.meaning: A switch turns electricity on and off. Press it one way and the light comes on. Press it the other way and the light goes off.
terms.example: You press the switch to turn on the fan.
terms.art: A finger pressing a switch on a switch board, and a tube light glowing above.

terms.meaning: A conductor is a material that lets electricity pass through it. Metals are good conductors. Water with salt in it is a conductor too, and so is the human body.
terms.example: The copper inside a wire is a conductor.
terms.art: A cut wire showing shiny orange copper strands inside the plastic cover.

terms.meaning: An insulator is a material that does not let electricity pass through easily. Plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood are insulators.
terms.example: The plastic cover on a wire is an insulator. It keeps the electricity inside.
terms.art: A wire with a thick coloured plastic cover, and a hand holding the plastic part of a plug.

terms.meaning: An electric shock happens when strong electricity flows through a person's body. It can burn, stop the heart, or kill.
terms.example: Touching a broken wire can give you an electric shock.
terms.art: A broken wire with bare copper showing, and a big red warning sign beside it.

terms.meaning: The main switch turns off the electricity for the whole home. It is in a box near the front door or in the meter room.
terms.example: In a flood, a grown-up turns off the main switch.
terms.art: A grey box of small black switches on a wall near a front door, out of a child's reach.

explanations.concept: Why the wall is dangerous and a cell is not
explanations.context: This card explains the difference between a torch cell and the wall socket.
explanations.definition: The push that drives electricity is measured in volts. A torch cell gives about 1.5 volts. Mains electricity in India is about 230 volts.
explanations.description: A torch cell pushes electricity very gently. You can touch both ends of a torch cell and feel nothing. The wall pushes about 150 times harder. That is strong enough to drive electricity through a person. So sockets, plugs and mains wires are for grown-ups only.
examples: A TV remote runs on two small cells. You can change them yourself.
The iron, the geyser and the washing machine run on mains electricity. Only a grown-up plugs them in.
Never put a small round button cell in your mouth or nose. If one is swallowed, it can burn the inside of the body. Tell a grown-up at once.
explanations.art: One torch cell on one side, and a row of many torch cells stretching across the page on the other side, next to a wall socket.

explanations.concept: Electricity travels through some things and not others
explanations.context: This card explains why wires have metal inside and plastic outside.
explanations.definition: A conductor lets electricity pass. An insulator does not let it pass easily.
explanations.description: Electricity flows along the metal inside a wire. Metal is a conductor. The plastic around the metal is an insulator, and it keeps the electricity away from your hand. If the plastic is cracked or burnt, the metal shows, and touching it can give you a shock. Salty water and your body are conductors too.
examples: Copper wire is a conductor. Its plastic cover is an insulator.
An electrician's screwdriver has a thick plastic handle, so electricity does not reach their hand.
A wet cloth on a wire is dangerous, because the water in the cloth can carry electricity.
explanations.art: A wire cut open, with a label on the copper saying 'conductor' and a label on the plastic saying 'insulator'.

explanations.concept: Why water and electricity are a dangerous pair
explanations.context: This card explains why we keep water away from switches, sockets and chargers.
explanations.definition: Water from a tap, rain or sweat always has some salt and other things mixed into it, so it carries electricity.
explanations.description: Dry skin does not let electricity in easily. Wet skin lets it in much more easily. So a wet hand on a switch is far more dangerous than a dry one. In the Dry Hands Test, a towel is the way to get hands really dry. Spilled water can also run into a socket or charger and carry electricity out to you.
examples: Never touch a switch straight after a bath or after playing in the rain.
Never use a phone while it is charging in the bathroom.
Keep glasses of water and juice away from the extension board.
explanations.art: A wet hand with drops falling, reaching towards a switch, and a red cross over it. Beside it, a hand being dried on a towel, with a green tick.

explanations.concept: Why a bird can sit on a wire
explanations.context: This card explains how a crow can sit on an electric wire and stay safe.
explanations.definition: Electricity flows through something only when it has a path to somewhere else, such as the ground or another wire.
explanations.description: A crow on a wire touches only that one wire. The electricity has nowhere else to go through the crow, so it stays in the wire. A person on a ladder who touches the wire is also touching the ground. Then the electricity has a path through the person. A big bird whose wings touch two wires at once can be killed.
examples: Crows, pigeons and mynas sit on wires all over Indian cities.
Never pull down a kite caught on a wire.
Never touch a fallen wire in the street, even if it looks dead.
explanations.art: A crow sitting on one wire with both feet, and a kite stuck on a wire with a string hanging down to a child, crossed out in red.

explanations.concept: What a shock does to a body
explanations.context: This card explains what happens inside a person who gets an electric shock.
explanations.definition: Your nerves carry tiny electric messages that tell your muscles and heart what to do. A shock is far stronger than these messages.
explanations.description: Your brain sends tiny electric messages along your nerves. They tell your muscles when to move. A shock is much, much stronger. It can make muscles grip tight, so a hand may not let go of a wire. It can also stop the heart from beating properly and burn the skin. That is why nobody should touch a person getting a shock until a grown-up has switched off the electricity.
examples: If you see someone stuck to a machine, do not touch them. Shout for a grown-up.
The grown-up switches off at the switch board or the main switch, then calls for a doctor.
A doctor can check the heartbeat with a machine called an ECG, which reads the heart's own tiny electric signals.
explanations.art: A simple drawing of a child's body with a thin glowing line from the brain down the arm to the hand, showing a nerve message.

agreed.text: Mains electricity can kill. Children should not touch sockets, plugs, wires or mains machines.
agreed.evidence: India's official records list thousands of deaths from electric shock every year. Most happen when someone touches a broken wire, a wet switch or a fallen line.

agreed.text: Wet skin lets electricity into the body much more easily than dry skin.
agreed.evidence: Engineers have measured how well skin carries electricity. Wet skin carries it many times better than dry skin. Safety rules everywhere say to keep switches dry and hands dry.

agreed.text: The human body carries electricity, because it is mostly water with salt in it.
agreed.evidence: In 1730, Stephen Gray in England showed that electricity could pass along a boy's body to his hand. Today, machines that read the heartbeat work by picking up the tiny electric signals in our own bodies.

challenging.claim: A small shock from a socket is harmless.
challenging.for: Some people have felt a small tingle from a switch and been fine.
challenging.against: The same socket can give a deadly shock if your hand is wet or you are standing on a wet floor. Nobody can tell beforehand which shock will be small.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea about small shocks.

challenging.claim: If someone is getting a shock, pull them away quickly.
challenging.who: What many people think in a hurry
challenging.for: It feels right to help a friend straight away.
challenging.against: If you touch them, the electricity can flow into you too. The safe way is to switch off the electricity first, then help.
challenging.context: This card is about what to do when someone gets a shock.

challenging.claim: Plastic plug-in covers keep small children safe from sockets.
challenging.for: In homes where sockets have no shutters, a cover can stop a toddler poking a pin or a key into the holes.
challenging.against: Some safety experts in the UK say covers are not needed in sockets that already have shutters inside. A badly fitting cover can even hold the shutters open. They say shuttered sockets and watching small children work better.
challenging.context: This card is about a real disagreement on keeping toddlers safe.

challenging.claim: Rubber chappals stop you getting a shock.
challenging.for: Rubber is an insulator, so a thick, dry rubber sole does make a shock less likely.
challenging.against: Chappals get wet, worn and thin. Your hand can still touch another path, like a wet wall or a steel tap. Chappals are never a reason to touch something electric.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea about rubber and shocks.

big_questions.q: Your body carries electricity, and your nerves send tiny electric messages. Is the electricity in you the same as the electricity in the wall?
big_questions.hint: Think about what is the same (it is the same force) and what is different (how strong it is, and what it does).

big_questions.q: In the Dry Hands Test, your hand sometimes felt dry but the paper showed it was wet. When should we trust our feelings, and when should we test?
big_questions.hint: Think about times when a test told you something your senses missed.

big_questions.q: A crow sits on a wire every day and is safe. You would not be. What makes the same wire safe for one and dangerous for another?
big_questions.hint: Think about where each body touches, and whether electricity can find a path through it.

big_questions.q: People made mains electricity, and it changed how we live. What would a day be like with no electricity at all?
big_questions.hint: Think about light at night, cooking, water pumps, phones and hospitals.

big_questions.q: Rules keep us safe. But who decides a rule, and how do they know it is right?
big_questions.hint: Think about how people found out that water carries electricity, and how tests can check a rule.

story.title: Tara and the Paper Hands
story.note: Tara, Kiran, Amma and Ammamma are made up. A. Lalitha was a real engineer from Chennai. The facts in the story are true: mains electricity can kill, water helps it into the body, and a crow on one wire is safe because the electricity has no path through them.
text: Tara was seven. She lived in a flat on the third floor in Kochi, with Amma and her grandmother, Ammamma.
Amma was a lineworker for the electricity board. She climbed electric poles and mended wires. Tara thought she had the bravest job in Kerala.
One evening in the monsoon, the rain came down so hard that the street looked like a river. Tara stood on the balcony and floated paper boats in a bucket of rainwater.
Inside, the room was getting dark. Tara ran in, dripping, and reached for the light switch.
'Stop!' said Ammamma. 'Your hands are wet.'
Tara shook her hands hard, flick, flick, flick. Then she rubbed them on her frock. 'Now they are dry,' she said.
Just then the door opened and Amma came in. Her raincoat was streaming. A tree had fallen on the wires in the next street, and she had been out fixing them with her team.
'Are they dry?' asked Amma. 'Let's ask the paper.'
She took an old newspaper from the shelf and laid it on the table. 'Press your hand flat on it. Count to three. Then lift it.'
Tara pressed. When she lifted her hand, there were five dark, damp fingerprints on the newspaper, and a damp patch where her palm had been.
'But they felt dry!' said Tara.
'Water can sit on your skin in a layer too thin to notice,' said Amma. She gave Tara a towel. 'Rub the front and the back. Count to ten.'
Tara rubbed and counted. Then she pressed her hand on a fresh part of the paper. This time, nothing. The paper stayed dry.
'Why does it matter so much?' asked Tara.

Amma sat down and took off her wet boots. 'The electricity in the wall is very strong. It can travel through water. It can travel through people too, because our bodies are mostly salty water. Dry skin keeps most of it out. Wet skin lets it in. That is why we never touch a switch with wet hands.'
'But you touch wires all the time,' said Tara.
'Only when the electricity is switched off,' said Amma. 'We check it twice. And we wear thick rubber gloves, because rubber is an insulator. Electricity does not pass through it easily.'
Tara looked out of the window. A row of crows sat on the wet wire outside, fluffing their feathers.
'Then why don't the crows get a shock?' she asked.

'Each crow touches only one wire,' said Amma. 'The electricity has nowhere else to go through them, so it stays in the wire. If I stood on a ladder and touched that wire, the electricity could go through me, down the ladder, to the ground. That is the danger.'
Ammamma brought in hot tea and banana fritters. 'Tell her about Lalitha,' she said.

'A. Lalitha grew up in Chennai, about a hundred years ago,' said Amma. 'Her husband died when she was only eighteen, and she had a baby daughter. People told her to stay at home. Instead, she studied electrical engineering at the college in Guindy. In the 1940s she became one of the first women engineers in India. Later she worked on the electrical equipment for the great Bhakra Nangal dam.'
'Like you,' said Tara.
'Well, I climb the poles,' laughed Amma. 'She designed the big machines.'

Just then the doorbell rang. It was Tara's cousin Kiran, who was five. He lived in the flat below. He had been jumping in puddles in the car park, and his hands and feet were soaking. He ran straight to the switch board to turn on the fan.
'Stop, Kiran!' said Tara. 'Your hands are wet.'
'I'll shake them,' said Kiran, and shook them.
Tara smiled. 'Let's ask the paper,' she said. She laid the newspaper on the table. 'Press your hand flat. Count to three.'
Kiran pressed, and lifted, and stared at his five wet fingerprints.
'Now the towel,' said Tara. 'Front and back. Count to ten with me.'
They counted together. Then Kiran pressed his hand on a fresh corner of the paper, and it stayed dry. He pressed the switch, and the fan began to turn.
Amma and Ammamma looked at each other and smiled.
story.epiphany: Tara's hands felt dry after shaking and wiping, but the paper showed wet fingerprints. She sees that you cannot always trust how your skin feels, so she tests with the paper. Then she understands why a wet hand on a switch is dangerous: water and her own body can carry electricity.
ask: Why did Ammamma stop Tara from touching the switch?
How did the newspaper show that Tara's hands were still wet?
Why can the crows sit on the wire, when Amma could not touch it from a ladder?
How did Tara help Kiran? What did she do first?

A woman in a dripping raincoat watching a girl lift her hand from a newspaper, which shows five damp fingerprints.
A row of crows on a wet electric wire outside a window, seen from inside a flat where a girl and her mother sit with tea.
A girl and a small boy pressing their hands on a newspaper on a table, with a towel beside them.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that electricity can travel along some things and through a person? This card tells the true story of Stephen Gray.
how_we_found_out.story: About 300 years ago, people knew that a glass tube rubbed with a cloth could attract feathers and bits of paper. They thought this power stayed inside the rubbed glass, like a smell stays in a flower. Stephen Gray did not have much money. He worked as a dyer of cloth in England, and studied science in his spare time. In 1729, he tied a long thread to a rubbed glass tube. To his surprise, the far end of the thread attracted feathers too. The electricity had travelled along the thread. His friend Granvile Wheler helped him hang the thread on silk loops. Silk kept the electricity on the thread. Brass wire let it escape. In 1730, Gray hung a boy from silk ropes and touched the rubbed tube to his feet. Bits of paper jumped up to the boy's hands. Electricity had passed through a human body. So the old idea was wrong. Electricity can move from one thing to another, through some materials and not through others.
how_we_found_out.who: Stephen Gray, a cloth dyer and self-taught scientist in England, with his friend Granvile Wheler
how_we_found_out.when: 1729 (the thread) and 1730 (the boy hung from silk ropes)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: The power of a rubbed glass tube stays inside the glass and cannot travel to anything else.
how_we_found_out.art: A boy hanging flat in the air from silk ropes in an old room, with a man holding a glass tube near his feet and small bits of paper rising towards the boy's hand.

experiments.title: The Dry Hands Test: how dry are your hands, really?
experiments.context: In this experiment your child wets their hand and dries it in four different ways. After each way, they press the hand on newspaper. Wet skin leaves dark, damp prints. So the paper shows which way really dries a hand before it touches a switch.
experiments.question: After you wash your hands, which way of drying them leaves no water on your skin: shaking, wiping on your clothes, or a towel?
experiments.predict: Which way will leave no wet print on the paper? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same hand and the same bowl of water every time. We dip the hand for the same count of 3. We press it on a fresh part of the paper for a count of 3. We dry for about the same time each way: five hard shakes, or a count of 10 on the clothes or the towel. Only one thing changes: the way we dry the hand.

materials.item: a few sheets of old newspaper, or paper napkins
a steel bowl of water from the tap
a dry hand towel
a pencil

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw round each wet print with a pencil before it dries, and write under it how you dried your hand.

setup.art: A steel bowl of water, a towel and sheets of newspaper laid on a table.
setup.caption: 1. Put out the bowl, the towel and the newspaper.

setup.art: A child dipping one hand into a steel bowl of water.
setup.caption: 2. Dip your hand in the water for a count of 3.

setup.art: A child shaking a wet hand, then wiping a hand on her frock, then rubbing a hand with a towel, shown as three small pictures.
setup.caption: 3. Dry it one way: shake, wipe on clothes, or use a towel.

setup.art: A child's hand lifting off a newspaper, leaving dark damp fingerprints, with pencil lines drawn round them.
setup.caption: 4. Press it on the paper. Draw round any wet prints.

flow.do: 1. Lay the newspaper flat on a table. 2. Fill a steel bowl with tap water. 3. Put the towel nearby. 4. Draw a results table on paper, with one row for each way of drying.
flow.say: We are going to find out how dry your hands really are. The newspaper will tell us. Wet skin leaves dark, damp marks on it.
flow.kid: Put out the bowl, the towel and the paper. Wet skin leaves dark marks on paper.

flow.do: Show the four ways of drying. Ask for a guess and a reason for each one. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will try four ways. Not dried, shaken five times, wiped on your clothes, and rubbed with a towel. Which ones will leave a wet print? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Which ways will leave wet prints? Why do you think so?

good: Shaking gets rid of the water, so no print.
Clothes soak up water like a towel.
Only the towel, because it is made for drying.

flow.parent: Write each guess down before you start. Many children guess that shaking or a wipe on clothes is enough. That is a good guess. Let the paper answer it.

flow.do: 1. Your child dips one hand for a count of 3. 2. They lift it out and do not dry it. 3. They say if it feels wet. 4. They press it flat on the paper for a count of 3, then lift. 5. Draw round the prints at once.
flow.say: First, no drying at all. Does it feel wet? Press it flat on the paper. One, two, three. Lift. What do you see?
flow.kid: Dip your hand. Do not dry it. Press it on the paper. Count to 3. Lift.
flow.parent: Damp patches fade within a minute, so draw round them quickly. If the marks are hard to see, hold the paper up to the window. Wet paper looks see-through.

flow.do: 1. Dip the same hand again. 2. Shake it hard five times. 3. Ask if it feels wet. 4. Press on a fresh part of the paper. 5. Draw round the prints. Count the wet fingerprints.
flow.say: Now dip and shake, five times. Does it feel wet now? Press it on a new part of the paper. How many wet fingerprints can you count?
flow.kid: Dip your hand. Shake it five times. Press it on new paper. Count the wet fingers.

flow.do: 1. Dip again. 2. Wipe the hand on your clothes, front and back, for a count of 10. 3. Ask if it feels wet. 4. Press on fresh paper. 5. Draw round and count.
flow.say: Now dip and wipe on your clothes, front and back. Count to ten. Does it feel dry? Press it. What does the paper say?
flow.kid: Dip your hand. Wipe it on your clothes. Count to 10. Press it on new paper.

flow.do: 1. Dip again. 2. Rub the hand with the towel, front, back and between the fingers, for a count of 10. 3. Press on fresh paper. 4. Draw round and count.
flow.say: Last, dip and use the towel. Rub the front, the back and between your fingers. Count to ten. Press it. What happens this time?
flow.kid: Dip your hand. Rub it with the towel. Count to 10. Press it on new paper.

flow.do: Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why. Then tell them why this matters for switches.
flow.say: Which way left no wet prints? Did any hand feel dry but leave a print? Water carries electricity, and wet skin lets it into your body. So we dry our hands with a towel before we touch any switch.
flow.kid: Which way left no wet prints? Did your hand feel dry but still leave a print?

good: Shaking still left wet prints.
My hand felt dry after my clothes, but some fingers were wet.
Only the towel left no prints.

ask.q: So what will you do before touching a switch?
good: Dry my hands with a towel first.
Use a towel, not my clothes.

flow.parent: Most children find that shaking leaves clear wet prints, and that a quick wipe on clothes often leaves damp fingertips even when the hand feels dry. A towel for a count of 10 usually leaves no print. If your child's clothes dried the hand well, that is a real result too. Point out that in a hurry, people rarely wipe for a full count of 10.

check.q: Your hand feels dry after you wipe it on your clothes. What is the safest thing to do before you press a switch?
options: Press the switch, because it feels dry
Dry it properly with a towel first
check.why: In the test, a hand can feel dry but still leave wet prints. A towel dries it properly. Wet skin lets electricity in much more easily.

experiments.title: The Spill Test: how far does one tumbler of water run?
experiments.context: In this experiment your child knocks over half a tumbler of water on the floor and on a towel, and measures how far it runs. A paper drawing of an extension board sits nearby. Did the spill reach it? This shows why drinks must stay far from sockets and chargers.
experiments.question: If a half-full tumbler of water falls over, how far will the water run?
experiments.predict: How many hand spans will the water run on the smooth floor? Will it reach the paper board two hand spans away? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same tumbler and the same amount of water each time. We tip it over the same way, from standing, as if knocked by an elbow. Only the place changes: the smooth floor or a folded towel.
results_table: Did it reach the paper board?

materials.item: a steel tumbler
water, to fill the tumbler half full
a smooth floor, such as the kitchen or bathroom floor
an old towel, folded in two
a paper drawing of an extension board, the size of your hand
a mop or an old cloth to wipe up

experiments.safety: Do this on a floor with no switches, sockets or wires nearby. Wipe the floor dry straight after each spill, so nobody slips.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the floor, the paper board and the puddle from above.

setup.art: A paper drawing of an extension board on a tiled floor, with a steel tumbler of water standing two hand spans away.
setup.caption: 1. Put the paper board two hand spans from the tumbler.

setup.art: A child's elbow knocking over a steel tumbler, and water rushing across a tiled floor towards the paper board.
setup.caption: 2. Knock the tumbler over, as if by accident.

setup.art: A child measuring a puddle with hand spans on the floor.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how far the water ran with your hand.

flow.do: 1. Choose a smooth floor with no sockets or wires near. 2. Your child draws an extension board on paper. 3. Put it two hand spans away from where the tumbler will stand.
flow.say: This paper is a pretend extension board. Real ones sit on the floor or on tables, with chargers and plugs in them. Let's see if a spill could reach it.
flow.kid: Draw an extension board on paper. Put it two hand spans away.
flow.parent: A hand span is the stretch from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger, with the hand spread wide. Use your child's hand every time.

flow.do: Fill the tumbler half full. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: If this tumbler falls over, how far will the water go? Will it reach the board? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: How far will the water run? Will it reach the board? Why?

good: Not far, because it is only half a tumbler.
Far, because water runs on a smooth floor.
It will stop quickly, because it is a small amount.

flow.do: 1. Stand the tumbler up, with the paper board two hand spans in front of it. 2. Your child kneels and knocks it over towards the board with an elbow. 3. Wait until the water stops moving. 4. Measure the longest run in hand spans. 5. Did it touch the paper board?
flow.say: Knock it with your elbow, like an accident at the table. Now let's wait until it stops. How many hand spans did it go?
flow.kid: Knock the tumbler over with your elbow. Wait. Measure with your hand.
flow.parent: Water on a smooth floor usually spreads much further than children expect, and splashes go further still. Then wipe the floor dry straight away.

flow.do: 1. Spread the folded towel on the floor, with the paper board two hand spans from the tumbler. 2. Fill the tumbler half full again. 3. Knock it over onto the towel, towards the board. 4. Measure how far the wet patch goes.
flow.say: Now the same spill onto a towel. Do you think it will go as far? Why?
flow.kid: Now knock it over onto the towel. Measure the wet patch.

flow.do: Wipe up. Ask what your child thinks, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: Where did the water go furthest? Did it reach the board? If that board had been real, the water could have carried electricity out of it. So where should we keep our drinks?
flow.kid: Where did the water go furthest? Where should drinks go?

good: Far away from the extension board.
On a different table from the charger.
Not on the floor next to the plugs.

flow.parent: The towel soaks up the water, so the spill stays small. A smooth floor or table lets it run. If your child's spill did not reach the board, move the board one hand span closer and try again. The point is that a spill can travel.

activities.title: Birds on the Wire: a window watch
activities.context: In this activity your child looks out of a window or balcony at the electric wires outside. They count the birds sitting on them, and draw how each bird sits. Then you talk about why the birds are safe and people are not.

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of electric wires or cables
paper and a pencil

activities.record: A drawing of the wire and every bird you saw sitting there, and a tally of how many birds you saw.

setup.art: A child at a flat's window looking at electric wires with crows and pigeons sitting on them.
setup.caption: 1. Look out at the wires. Count the birds.

setup.art: A child's drawing of one wire with five birds sitting along the wire, each with both feet on the same wire, and a tally beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each bird on the wire.

flow.do: Find a window or balcony where you can see wires. Count the birds on them for two minutes.
flow.say: Let's watch the wires for two minutes. Make a tally mark for every bird you see sitting on a wire.
flow.kid: Watch the wires. Make a mark for every bird you see.
flow.parent: Crows, pigeons, mynas and sparrows often sit on wires. Early morning and evening are good times. If you cannot see any wires from home, draw the crows you remember seeing on wires.

flow.do: Your child draws the wire and the birds. Ask them to look closely at the feet.
flow.say: Draw the wire and each bird. Look at their feet. How many wires does each bird touch?
flow.kid: Draw the birds. How many wires does each bird touch?

ask.q: How many wires does each bird touch?
good: Just one.
Both feet are on the same wire.

flow.do: Ask for your child's idea first. Then explain.
flow.say: Why do you think the birds are safe? Each bird touches only one wire. The electricity has nowhere else to go through them. A person on a ladder touches the ground too. Then the electricity can go through them.
flow.kid: Why are the birds safe? Why would a person not be safe?

ask.q: Why would a person on a ladder not be safe?
good: The ladder and their feet touch the ground.
The electricity could go through them to the ground.

flow.parent: Big birds with wide wings, such as peacocks or eagles, can be killed if their wings touch two wires at once. Never let your child pull at a kite or string caught on a wire.

activities.title: Safety Helpers in Our Home
activities.context: In this activity a grown-up shows your child the things in your home that keep electricity where it belongs: the plastic on wires, the plastic body of a plug, the shutters inside a socket, and the main switch. Your child looks but does not touch, then draws each helper.

materials.item: an unplugged machine with a plug, such as a mixer or table fan
a torch
paper and crayons

activities.record: A page of drawings, one for each safety helper, with a sentence saying what it does.

setup.art: A mother holding an unplugged plug and pointing to its plastic body and metal pins while a girl watches.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a plug and a wire. Find the plastic parts.

setup.art: A torch shining into a socket on a switch board, showing small plastic shutters behind the holes.
setup.caption: 2. Look at a socket with a torch. Do not touch.

setup.art: A grey box of small black switches on a wall near a front door, with a mother pointing up at it.
setup.caption: 3. Find the main switch box.

flow.do: 1. Unplug a mixer or table fan. 2. Show the plug and wire. 3. Point to the plastic body, the metal pins and the plastic cover on the wire.
flow.say: The metal pins carry the electricity. The plastic body is for holding. The plastic cover on the wire keeps the electricity inside. Why do you think the holder is plastic, not metal?
flow.kid: Look at the plug. Which part is metal? Which part is plastic?

good: Electricity does not go through plastic easily.
So it does not go into your hand.

flow.parent: Only you handle the plug. Always hold a plug by its plastic body, never pull it out by the wire.

flow.do: Shine a torch at a socket. Look for small plastic shutters behind the holes. Your child looks only.
flow.say: Many new sockets have little plastic doors inside. They open only when a plug's pins push in together. They stop a small child poking a pin in. Can you see them?
flow.kid: Look at the socket with the torch. Can you see little doors? Do not touch.
flow.parent: Not every socket has shutters. Older ones often do not. If yours do not, that is a reason to keep small children well away.

flow.do: Show your child the main switch box from where they stand. Do not open it.
flow.say: This box turns off the electricity for the whole home. Some boxes also have a safety switch that turns off by itself if electricity leaks out. In a flood or a fire, a grown-up turns it off here.
flow.kid: This box can turn off all the electricity. Only grown-ups use it.
flow.parent: Many Indian homes now have small switches called MCBs, and some have a safety switch called an RCCB or ELCB. An RCCB switches off in a fraction of a second if electricity leaks, for example through a person. Ask an electrician whether your home has one.

flow.do: Your child draws each helper and says what it does. You write the sentence.
flow.say: Draw each helper we found. Tell me what it does, and I will write it down.
flow.kid: Draw each safety helper. Say what it does.

activities.title: What Do We Do If...? an act-out
activities.context: In this activity your child acts out what to do when something goes wrong with electricity. A grown-up reads a card, and the child shows what they would do. The rule in every case is the same: do not touch, move away, and call a grown-up.

materials.item: five small pieces of paper, one for each scene in the steps
a string or dupatta on the floor, to be a pretend wire

activities.record: Your child tells someone else in the family the three steps: do not touch, move away, call a grown-up.

setup.art: A mother reading a card aloud while a girl stands beside a dupatta lying on the floor like a fallen wire.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up reads a card.

setup.art: The girl stepping back from the dupatta with her hands up, calling out towards a door.
setup.caption: 2. Show what you would do. Step back and call for help.

flow.do: Lay the dupatta on the floor as a pretend wire. Read the first card: 'You see a wire lying on the road after a storm.'
flow.say: Here is a fallen wire after a storm. What would you do? Show me.
flow.kid: A wire is lying on the road. What do you do? Show it.

good: Do not touch it.
Walk far away from it.
Tell a grown-up.

flow.parent: Fallen wires can still carry electricity. Water around them can carry it too. Keep well back, and tell the electricity board.

flow.do: Read the card: 'You see sparks and smell burning from a socket.'
flow.say: The socket is sparking. What would you do?
flow.kid: Sparks come from a socket. What do you do?

good: Move away.
Call a grown-up to switch off the main switch.
Never throw water on it.

flow.parent: Never throw water on an electrical fire. Switch off the main switch first.

flow.do: Read the card: 'Your friend is touching a machine and cannot let go.'
flow.say: Your friend is stuck to a machine. What would you do? Would you pull them away?
flow.kid: Your friend is stuck to a machine. What do you do?

good: No, the electricity could go into me too.
I would shout for a grown-up to switch it off.

flow.do: Read the card: 'Your kite is caught on an electric wire.'
flow.say: Your kite is stuck on a wire. What would you do?
flow.kid: Your kite is stuck on a wire. What do you do?

good: Let go of the string.
Leave the kite there.
Never climb or pull it.

flow.do: Read the card: 'A baby is crawling towards a socket.'
flow.say: A baby is crawling near a socket. What would you do?
flow.kid: A baby crawls to a socket. What do you do?

good: Pick up a toy to call the baby away.
Call a grown-up at once.

flow.parent: Finish by asking your child to say the three steps aloud: do not touch, move away, call a grown-up.

games.title: Safe Steps: a snakes and ladders game about electricity
games.players: 2 to 4 players. A grown-up plays too.
games.context: This is a board game like snakes and ladders, a game first played in India. Some squares show a safe thing to do, with a ladder up. Others show a dangerous thing, with a snake down. Each time you land on one, you say why it is safe or dangerous.

printables.title: Board of 25 squares, 5 rows of 5
items: Square 1: Start.
Square 2: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 3: You dry your hands on a towel before you press the fan switch. Climb the ladder to square 11.
Square 4: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 5: You poke a hairpin at a socket. Slide down the snake to square 1.
Square 6: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 7: You tell a grown-up that the iron's wire is cracked. Climb the ladder to square 14.
Square 8: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 9: You pull a plug out by its wire. Slide down the snake to square 4.
Square 10: You keep your juice on a different table from the charger. Climb the ladder to square 16.
Square 11: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 12: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 13: You touch the light switch straight after your bath. Slide down the snake to square 6.
Square 14: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 15: You let go of your kite when it gets stuck on a wire. Climb the ladder to square 21.
Square 16: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 17: You use your phone while it charges in the bathroom. Slide down the snake to square 8.
Square 18: You call a grown-up when you see sparks. Climb the ladder to square 23.
Square 19: You pull a friend away from a machine that is giving a shock. Slide down the snake to square 14.
Square 20: You touch a wire lying on the road after the rain. Slide down the snake to square 12.
Square 21: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 22: You call a grown-up when your little cousin plays with a plug. Climb the ladder to square 24.
Square 23: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 24: Plain square. Say one electricity rule you know, or just rest.
Square 25: Finish. You are a safety expert.

rules: Cut out the 25 squares. Lay them in 5 rows of 5, with square 1 at the bottom left. Number the rows from the bottom, and go left to right in every row.
Each player needs a button or a coin as a counter. You also need one dice, or six paper slips marked 1 to 6 to pick from.
Everyone starts on square 1. Take turns to roll the dice and move your counter.
If you land on a ladder square, read the square aloud. Say why it is safe. Then climb to the square the ladder leads to.
If you land on a snake square, read the square aloud. Say why it is dangerous. Then slide down to the square the snake leads to.
On a plain square, say one electricity rule you know. If you do not know one, just rest.
If you cannot say why, the grown-up helps, and you still move.
The first player to reach square 25, or to roll past it, wins.

setup.art: 25 cut-out squares laid in 5 rows of 5 on a big sheet, with pencil lines for ladders and snakes and small pictures of a towel, a socket and a kite.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the 25 squares and join each ladder or snake to the square where the line ends.

setup.art: Children sitting on the floor round the board, one rolling a dice and another moving a button up a ladder.
setup.caption: 2. Roll, move, and say why when you land on a snake or ladder.

flow.do: Cut out the 25 squares and lay them in 5 rows of 5. Draw a line from each ladder or snake square to the square where the line ends.
flow.say: Let us build the board. The ladders are safe things to do. The snakes are dangerous things.
flow.kid: Lay out the squares. Ladders are safe. Snakes are dangerous.

flow.do: Play. Each time a player lands on a special square, they say why.
flow.say: You landed on a snake. Read it. Why is that dangerous?
flow.kid: Read your square. Say why it is safe or dangerous.

ask.q: Why is touching a switch after your bath dangerous?
good: My hands are wet.
Water lets electricity into my body.

ask.q: Why is it good to tell a grown-up about a cracked wire?
good: The metal shows through.
Someone could get a shock.

flow.do: After the game, ask which snake would be most dangerous in real life.
flow.say: Which snake would be the most dangerous in real life? Why?
flow.kid: Which snake is the most dangerous in real life? Why?

check.q: In the game, you pulled a friend away from a machine giving a shock. Why is that a snake?
options: The electricity can flow into you too
check.why: If you touch someone getting a shock, the electricity can pass into you. A grown-up must switch off the electricity first.

games.title: Live Wire Freeze: a moving game
games.players: 1 or more children, and a grown-up who calls the cards
games.context: This is a moving game. Players walk or dance round the room. The caller reads a card. If the card shows something dangerous, everyone freezes and shouts the safe thing to do. If it is safe, everyone keeps moving.

items.f: Someone pokes a key into a socket.
items.b: Danger. Freeze and shout: Never poke anything into a socket.

items.f: Someone dries their hands on a towel, then switches on the light.
A kite is stuck on a wire, and someone pulls the string.
items.b: Danger. Freeze and shout: Let go. Leave the kite.

items.f: Someone changes the cells in the TV remote.
items.b: Safe. Keep moving. Cells are weak and safe to hold.

items.f: Water is spilled next to the extension board.
items.b: Danger. Freeze and shout: Move away. Call a grown-up.

items.f: A grown-up holds the plug by its plastic body to unplug the mixer.
Someone sees a wire with the copper showing.
items.b: Danger. Freeze and shout: Do not touch. Tell a grown-up.

items.f: Crows sit on the wire outside.
items.b: Safe for the crows. Keep moving. They touch only one wire.

items.f: A wire is lying in a puddle after the rain.
items.b: Danger. Freeze and shout: Stay far away.

items.f: Someone reads a book under a lamp, with their water bottle on the floor far away.

rules: The grown-up is the caller. Everyone else walks, hops or dances round the room.
The caller reads a card aloud.
If it is dangerous, everyone freezes and shouts the safe thing to do.
If it is safe, everyone keeps moving.
Anyone who freezes on a safe card, or keeps moving on a danger card, says the reason. Then they carry on.
When all 10 cards have been read, the game is over. Shuffle the cards and play again if you like.

setup.art: Two children dancing in a room while a grown-up holds up a card.
setup.caption: 1. Move round the room while the caller reads.

setup.art: The two children frozen like statues with their hands up, shouting.
setup.caption: 2. Danger card: freeze and shout the safe thing to do.

flow.do: Cut out the cards and shuffle them. Clear a space on the floor.
flow.say: When I read a danger card, freeze like a statue and shout what to do. When it is safe, keep moving.
flow.kid: Move round. Freeze if it is danger. Shout the safe thing to do.

flow.do: Read the cards one by one. After each, read the back aloud.
flow.say: Someone pokes a key into a socket. Freeze! What do we shout?
flow.kid: Listen to the card. Freeze or keep moving?

ask.q: Why are cells in the remote safe?
good: They are weak.
The wall is much stronger than a cell.

projects.title: A Safety Picture Book for a Little One
projects.context: In this project your child makes a small picture book of electricity safety rules for a younger child: a little brother, sister, cousin or neighbour. Teaching a rule is a good way to understand it.

materials.item: two sheets of paper, folded and stapled to make an eight-page book
crayons or sketch pens
a stapler or a needle and thread, used by a grown-up

schedule.what: Choose six rules. Draw one rule on each page.
Write a few words under each picture. Read the book to a younger child.

projects.record: The finished book, and one sentence about what the younger child asked.

setup.art: Two sheets of paper folded in half and stapled into a small book, with a cover saying 'Safe with Electricity'.
setup.caption: 1. Fold and staple the paper into a book.

setup.art: A girl of seven reading her picture book to a small boy, pointing at a drawing of a socket with a red cross.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a rule on each page, then read it to a little one.

flow.do: Fold and staple the book. Help your child choose six rules.
flow.say: Which six rules matter most for a little child? Let's choose them together.
flow.kid: Choose six rules for a little child.

flow.do: Your child draws one rule on each page, with a green tick for safe and a red cross for danger.
flow.say: Draw one rule on each page. A green tick for the safe way, a red cross for the dangerous way.
flow.kid: Draw one rule on each page. Use a tick or a cross.

flow.do: Your child says a few words for each page. Write them, or let your child write one or two words.
flow.say: What do you want the page to say? Keep it short, so a little one understands.
flow.kid: Say a few words for each page. Keep them short.

flow.do: Your child reads the book to a younger child, or to a toy if no little one is near.
flow.say: Now you are the teacher. Read it slowly and point at each picture.
flow.kid: Read your book to a little one. Point at each picture.

ask.q: What did the little one ask?
good: Why can't I touch the socket?
Why are crows safe?

challenges.title: The Safe Homework Corner
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge. Meenakshi, a girl in Class 2, is setting up a homework corner. She has a table, a lamp with a plug, a phone charger, a water bottle and a cup of paint water. Where should everything go, so nothing wet can reach the plugs?
challenges.problem: Draw a plan of a homework corner where the lamp and the charger are safe from spills.
constraints: There is only one extension board, and at the start it sits on the floor under the table.
Meenakshi needs her water bottle and her paint water while she works.
The lamp's wire must not stretch across where people walk.
materials: small paper cut-outs of a lamp, a charger, a bottle and a cup, to move around
general: Keep the water bottle and paint water at the far end of the table, away from the lamp and the plugs.
Lift the extension board off the floor, onto a dry shelf, so a spill on the floor cannot reach it.
Put the paint water in a wide, low bowl that is hard to knock over.
creative: Put the drinks on a tray with a rim, so a spill stays on the tray.
Do painting on a different table, away from the lamp.
Stick a 'dry hands' sign with a towel hook next to the switch.
challenges.your_turn: Now plan your own homework corner, or the place where you do this unit. Draw where each thing goes, and mark the path a spill would take.

setup.art: A plan of a table seen from above, with paper cut-outs of a lamp, a charger, a water bottle and a cup of paint water.
setup.caption: 1. Move the paper cut-outs around the table plan.

setup.art: The same plan with the water things at one end and the lamp and plugs at the other, and an arrow showing a spill running off the edge away from the plugs.
setup.caption: 2. Draw where each thing goes, and the path a spill would take.

flow.do: Read the problem aloud. Draw the table from above.
flow.say: Meenakshi has a lamp, a charger, a water bottle and paint water. What could go wrong?
flow.kid: What could go wrong at Meenakshi's table?

good: The paint water could spill on the charger.
Water could run down to the extension board.

flow.do: Your child cuts out the things and moves them on the plan until they are happy. Then draws them in.
flow.say: Move the things around. Where would a spill go? Where is the safest place for each?
flow.kid: Move the things around. Where would a spill go?
flow.parent: If you did the Spill Test, remind your child how far half a tumbler ran.

flow.do: Talk about the usual answers and the creative ones. Then your child plans their own corner.
flow.say: Here are some ideas other people use. Which do you like? Now plan your own corner.
flow.kid: Which idea do you like best? Now plan your own corner.

videos.title: Be Safe with Electricity
videos.why: Shows in simple words why children do not touch sockets, plugs and wires, and why water and electricity must be kept apart.
videos.check: Found by search: "Be Safe with Electricity [CC]" by WonderGrove Kids, 2 minutes 46 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Why birds on power lines do not get zapped
videos.why: Shows birds on a wire and explains, with a simple drawing, that the electricity has no path through a bird touching one wire.
videos.check: Found by search: "Why Don't Birds on Power Lines Get Zapped?" by SciShow, 3 minutes 12 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Monsoon electrical safety guide
videos.why: Gives short monsoon safety advice from an Indian electricity company, including staying away from wires and water.
videos.check: Found by search: "Tata Power's Guide to Monsoon Electrical Safety" by Tata Power, 1 minute 19 seconds. A parent may preview it.

quiz.p: Why can you hold a torch cell, but must never touch the holes of a wall socket?
opts: The wall electricity is much stronger than a cell's
The cell is made of metal
quiz.why: A torch cell gives about 1.5 volts. The wall gives about 230 volts in India, about 150 times stronger. That is strong enough to hurt or kill a person.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 2, drops a hairpin near a socket. What should he do?
opts: Push the hairpin into the socket to keep it safe
Pick it up and never poke it into the socket
quiz.why: Never poke anything into a socket. A metal hairpin is a conductor, and it would carry the electricity into his hand.

quiz.p: In the Dry Hands Test, you dry a wet hand and press it on newspaper. Which way dries the hand properly?
opts: Rubbing it with a towel for a count of 10
quiz.why: Shaking leaves clear wet prints. A wipe on clothes often leaves damp fingertips. A towel dries the skin properly.

quiz.p: Why is a wet hand on a switch more dangerous than a dry one?
opts: Wet skin lets electricity into the body more easily
Water makes the switch slippery, and that is all
quiz.why: Water carries electricity, and wet skin lets it in much more easily than dry skin. So always dry your hands before touching a switch.

quiz.p: Your friend Lakshmi is touching a machine and cannot let go. What should you do first?
opts: Pull her away by the arm
Shout for a grown-up to switch off the electricity
quiz.why: If you touch her, the electricity can flow into you too. Water carries electricity. A grown-up must switch off the electricity first.

quiz.p: After a storm, Divya, a girl in Class 2, sees a wire lying in a puddle on the road. What should she do?
opts: Move it out of the way with her foot
Stay far away and tell a grown-up
quiz.why: A fallen wire can still carry mains electricity, and the puddle around it can carry it too. Keep far away and tell a grown-up, who calls the electricity board.

quiz.p: A crow sits on an electric wire and is safe. Why?
opts: The crow touches only one wire, so the electricity has no path through her
The wire is switched off whenever birds land
quiz.why: Electricity flows through something only when it has a path to somewhere else, like the ground or another wire. A crow on one wire gives the electricity no such path.

quiz.p: Anjali, a girl in Class 2, has a kite stuck on an electric wire. What is the safe thing to do?
opts: Let go of the string and leave the kite
quiz.why: A string, especially a wet one, can carry electricity from the wire to the person holding it. Climbing near wires is very dangerous. A new kite is easy to get.

quiz.p: Why is the wire of the table fan covered in plastic?
opts: Plastic is an insulator, so it keeps the electricity inside the wire
quiz.why: The metal inside the wire is a conductor. The plastic outside is an insulator. It keeps the electricity away from your hand.

quiz.p: There is a flood in the building, and water is coming into the flat. What should a grown-up do with the electricity?
opts: Turn off the main switch, if it can be reached without standing in water
Unplug every machine with wet hands
quiz.why: The main switch turns off electricity to the whole home. A grown-up turns it off if they can reach it safely and dry. Then the water in the flat cannot carry mains electricity.

worksheets.title: Water, wires and the Dry Hands Test

items.p: Draw a line from each rule to the reason for it.
pairs: Never poke anything into a socket
Metal things carry the electricity into your hand
Dry your hands with a towel first
Wet skin lets electricity into your body
items.why: Every rule has a reason. A child who knows the reason can work out what to do in a new place too.

items.p: Draw the prints from your Dry Hands Test. Draw one hand for each way of drying, and colour the wet parts.
items.a: Four hands, with wet prints for not dried and shaken, perhaps a few wet fingers for clothes, and no wet parts for the towel.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the four ways side by side, so you can see which one dried the hand. If your clothes worked well, draw what really happened.
items.art: Four empty hand outlines in a row, labelled 'not dried', 'shaken', 'clothes' and 'towel'.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: in the Dry Hands Test, did any hand feel dry but still leave a wet print? What does that tell you?
items.a: For example: 'Yes, after wiping on my frock. My hand felt dry but three fingers left wet marks. So I should use a towel, not my clothes.'
items.why: A strong answer uses what the paper showed as evidence, and says what to do because of it.

items.p: You feel a small tingle from a switch and nothing bad happens. So it is safe to keep touching it.
items.why: False. Nobody can tell beforehand which shock will be small. The same switch can give a bad shock if your hands are wet.

items.p: Sort these into 'a child can do this' and 'only a grown-up does this'.
items: press the light switch with dry hands
A child can do this
put a plug into a socket
Only a grown-up does this
change the cells in the TV remote
A child can do this
turn off the main switch
Only a grown-up does this
unplug the iron
Only a grown-up does this
switch on a torch
A child can do this
items.why: Cells are weak and safe. Switches are made to be pressed, with dry hands. Plugs, sockets and the main switch carry strong mains electricity, so grown-ups handle them.

items.p: Pooja, a girl in Class 2, says: "I wear rubber chappals, so I can touch a broken wire." Is she right?
opts: No, chappals can be wet or thin, and she could touch something else too
items.why: A dry, thick rubber sole helps, but chappals get wet and worn. Another part of her could touch a wet wall or a steel tap. Nobody should touch a broken wire.

items.p: Never touch a switch, a plug or a socket with ________ hands.
items.why: Wet skin lets electricity into the body much more easily than dry skin.

items.p: Three of these carry electricity. Which one does not carry it easily?
items.why: Copper and steel are metals, and metals are conductors. Salty water is a conductor too. Plastic is an insulator.

items.p: Label the plug: metal pins, plastic body, wire with plastic cover.
a: metal pins: the three prongs that go into the socket
plastic body: the part you hold
wire with plastic cover: the cable coming out of the back
items.why: The metal pins carry the electricity into the machine. The plastic parts are insulators, so they are the parts a grown-up holds.
items.art: A three-pin plug with its wire, and three empty label lines pointing to the pins, the body and the wire.

items.p: Meena is seven and lives in Hyderabad. She wants to switch on the fan herself. Her grandmother and her mother do not agree about it.

views.says: Children should never touch anything electric. Not even a switch.
Switches are made to be pressed. Meena can do it, if her hands are dry.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as 'switches have plastic covers and are made to be touched' or 'it is safest if children never touch anything'. Then it says something fair about the other view, such as 'Grandmother is right that sockets and plugs are dangerous'.
items.why: Both views care about Meena's safety. Switches are designed to be safe to press with dry hands. Sockets, plugs and wires are not for children.

worksheets.title: Birds, kites, spills and safety helpers

items.p: A pigeon sits on one electric wire. A man on a metal ladder touches the same wire. Who is in danger?
items.why: The man is also touching the ground through the ladder and his feet. So the electricity has a path through him. The pigeon touches only one wire.

items.p: Say it out loud, and a grown-up writes it: why is it dangerous to pull a kite string that is caught on an electric wire?
items.a: For example: 'The string touches the wire. If it is wet, electricity can go down the string into me and into the ground.'
items.why: A strong answer says the string makes a path from the wire to the person, and that wet string makes it worse.

items.p: Your friend is getting a shock from a machine. Put the steps in order.
items: A grown-up calls a doctor
Do not touch your friend
A grown-up switches off the electricity
Shout for a grown-up
a: A grown-up switches off the electricity
items.why: First keep yourself safe, so the electricity does not flow into you too. Then get help. The electricity must be off before anyone touches the person.

items.p: If water spills near a socket, wipe it up quickly with your hand.
items.why: False. Water near a socket may carry electricity. Move away and tell a grown-up. A grown-up switches off first, then dries it.

items.p: Draw your Spill Test from above: the floor, the paper extension board and the puddle. Show how far the water ran.
items.a: A floor with a tumbler on its side, a puddle spreading, and the paper board, with the puddle reaching it or nearly reaching it.

items.p: Draw a line from each safety helper to what it does.
pairs: Keeps the electricity inside the wire
Stop a small child poking something in
Turns off electricity for the whole home
Turns off by itself if electricity leaks out
items.why: Each helper keeps electricity in its proper path, or stops it quickly when something goes wrong.

items.p: Kiran, a boy aged five, says: "I can hold a torch cell, so the wall socket is safe too." Say what you would tell him, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: For example: 'A torch cell is weak. The wall is about 150 times stronger. It can go through your body and hurt you.'
items.why: A strong answer says that both give electricity, but the wall is far stronger, strong enough to pass through a person.

items.p: Why must drinks be kept away from the extension board?
opts: A spill can run into the board and carry electricity out to us
The board makes drinks taste bad
items.why: In the Spill Test, half a tumbler of water ran a long way on a smooth floor. Water can carry electricity from a socket to anyone touching the puddle.

items.p: Plastic and rubber are called ________, because electricity does not pass through them easily.
items.why: Insulators keep electricity where it belongs. That is why wires, plugs and switches have plastic on the outside.

items.p: Kavya's family in Chennai has a new baby. Kavya's mother and her aunt disagree about the sockets in the flat.

views.says: We should put plastic covers into every socket, so the baby cannot poke anything in.
Our new sockets already have shutters inside. Covers are not needed, and a loose cover can hold the shutters open. It is better to watch the baby and keep wires out of reach.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Why? Then say one thing the other person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with a reason, such as 'covers are an extra wall in old sockets with no shutters', or 'shutters already do the job, and covers can go wrong'. Then it says something fair about the other side.
items.why: This is a real disagreement among parents and safety experts. Covers may help in old sockets with no shutters. Some experts say they are not needed where sockets already have shutters.

items.p: An electrician's screwdriver has a thick plastic handle. Say why, and a grown-up writes it.
items.a: For example: 'Plastic is an insulator. If the metal tip touches electricity, it cannot pass through the handle into the hand.'
items.why: A strong answer names plastic as an insulator and says it keeps electricity away from the hand. Electricians also switch the electricity off first.

items.p: Your nerves use tiny electric signals. So the electricity in the wall is about the same size as those signals.
items.why: False. Nerve signals are tiny. The wall gives about 230 volts, strong enough to push electricity through a person.

items.p: Invent a new safety helper for a socket that a toddler cannot open. Draw it. A grown-up writes your label for how it works.
items.a: Any clear design, such as a socket with a cover that opens only with two hands, or a socket placed high up out of reach.
items.why: A strong design stops a small child reaching the holes but still lets a grown-up plug things in, and the label says how.

items.p: Sort these places for charging a phone into 'safe' and 'not safe'.
items: on a dry table away from water
Safe
on the edge of the kitchen sink
Not safe
on a wet bathroom shelf
Not safe
on a dry shelf in the hall
Safe
next to a vase of flowers with water
Not safe
items.why: A charger is plugged into mains electricity. It belongs where no water can spill on it or near it.

items.p: Very pure water carries electricity much better than salty water.
items.why: False. Very pure water carries electricity poorly. The salt and other things mixed into water are what let it carry electricity. Tap water, rain and sweat all have some mixed into them.

items.p: Stephen Gray hung his long thread on silk loops, and the electricity stayed on the thread. When he used brass wire, the electricity escaped. Which kind of material should cover the wires in our homes? Why?
items.a: For example: 'A material like silk or plastic, because it does not let electricity through. It keeps the electricity in the wire.'
items.why: A strong answer sees that silk worked like an insulator and brass like a conductor, and that wires need an insulator on the outside.

items.p: Label the picture: safe bird, dangerous kite string, path to the ground.
a: safe bird: the crow sitting on one wire
dangerous kite string: the string hanging from the wire to the boy's hand
path to the ground: from the wire, down the string, through the boy, to his feet
items.why: The crow touches one wire, so the electricity has no path through her. The string and the boy make a path from the wire to the ground.
items.art: A wire with a crow sitting there, and a kite caught on the same wire with its string hanging down to a boy standing on the ground, with three empty label lines.

items.p: A big bird opens their wings and touches two electric wires at the same time. What can happen?
opts: Nothing, because birds are always safe
Electricity can pass from one wire through the bird to the other wire, and hurt the bird
items.why: Now there is a path between two wires. A bird on one wire has no such path, so she is safe.

items.p: The wall socket in India gives about 230 volts. A torch cell gives about ________ volts.
items.why: A torch cell gives about 1.5 volts. 230 is about 150 times as much.

applications: Electricians switch off the power and check it twice before they touch any wire.
Lineworkers on electric poles wear thick rubber gloves and boots, because rubber is an insulator.
Bathrooms in many homes have their geyser switch outside the door, away from water.
Builders put safety switches called RCCBs in new flats, to turn off the power in a fraction of a second if it leaks.
Doctors read the heart's own tiny electric signals with an ECG machine.

open_questions.q: Why do some people live through a big shock while others do not?
open_questions.why_open: It depends on how strong the electricity was, its path through the body, how wet the skin was, and even the moment in the heartbeat. Doctors still cannot always say beforehand what a shock will do.

open_questions.q: How do electric eels make shocks stronger than our wall sockets without hurting themselves?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know eels have special organs that make the shock. Exactly how the eel's own body stays protected is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Which animals can sense electricity, and how?
open_questions.why_open: Sharks, platypuses and bumblebees can sense electricity, and scientists keep finding more animals who can. How many others do, and what it is like for them, is still being found out.

maths.problem: In the Dry Hands Test, Revathi, a girl in Class 2, got 5 wet fingerprints with no drying, 5 after shaking, 2 after wiping on her clothes, and 0 after the towel. How many fewer wet fingerprints did the towel leave than shaking?
maths.answer: 5 fewer. Shaking left 5 and the towel left 0.
maths.explain: 5 take away 0 is 5. So the towel left 5 fewer wet fingerprints than shaking.
maths.context: This is about the Dry Hands Test, where you pressed your hand on newspaper after drying it in different ways.
maths.why_maths: Taking away shows how much better one way of drying was than another.

maths.problem: In the Spill Test, the water ran 3 hand spans on the floor and less than 1 hand span on the towel. The paper board was 2 hand spans away. Did the floor spill reach the board? Did the towel spill?
maths.answer: The floor spill reached it, because 3 is more than 2. The towel spill did not, because less than 1 is less than 2.
maths.explain: Compare each run with 2. 3 is bigger than 2, so it reached. Less than 1 is smaller than 2, so it stopped short.
maths.context: This is about the Spill Test, where you knocked over half a tumbler and measured how far the water ran.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two numbers tells us whether a spill could reach a plug.

maths.problem: Ranjana, a girl in Class 2, counted the birds on the wire outside: 4 crows, 3 pigeons and 1 myna. How many birds were there? How many wires did each bird touch?
maths.answer: 8 birds. Each one touched just 1 wire.
maths.explain: 4 and 3 make 7, and 1 more makes 8. Every bird had both feet on the same wire, which is why they were safe.
maths.context: This is about the window watch, where you counted the birds sitting on electric wires.
maths.why_maths: Tally marks and adding help us count a group of birds that keep moving.

maths.problem: Gauri, a girl in Class 2, found these things at home: a TV remote, a fan, a wall clock, a fridge, a torch and an iron. Sort them into 'runs on cells' and 'runs on the wall'. Which group is bigger?
maths.answer: Cells: TV remote, wall clock, torch. Wall: fan, fridge, iron. Both groups have 3, so they are the same size.
maths.explain: Count each group. 3 and 3 are equal. The cell things are safe to hold. The wall things are plugged in by grown-ups.
maths.context: This is about sorting the electric things in a home by where their electricity comes from.
maths.why_maths: Sorting into groups and comparing them shows how many things in a home use strong mains electricity.

roots.context: We have tested how dry our hands really are, watched birds on wires, and learned why water and mains electricity must never meet. Now we ask what electricity tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: A hand can feel dry and still leave wet prints on paper. The water on it has salt in it, and salty water carries electricity. Your body is mostly water with salts in it. So electricity can pass through a person, and wet skin lets it in more easily.
deep_truth.habit: We think of electricity as something that belongs to wires and machines, and of our bodies as something different. But the body is made of the same kind of material that electricity travels through, and our nerves send tiny electric messages of their own.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dry Hands Test, shaking and wiping on clothes left damp prints on the paper. Water with salt in it carries electricity, and wet skin lets it in many times more easily than dry skin. In 1730, Stephen Gray showed electricity passing through a boy's body.

three.who_am_i: Much of you is salty water, and that carries electricity. Your own nerves send tiny electric messages all day.
three.what_is_life: Many living bodies use tiny electric signals. Your heartbeat, a bee sensing a flower, and a plant's leaf closing all use them.
three.what_is_this_world: The same electric force lights the fan, flashes as lightning, and carries messages in your body. Only the strength is different.

roots.thread: The electricity in the wall, the lightning in a monsoon sky and the tiny messages in your nerves are the same kind of force, at very different strengths. Your body is part of the electric world. It holds the water and salt that carry electricity. That is why mains electricity is dangerous to us: it can flow through us as it flows through a wire. Living beings also use this force gently. A touch-me-not folds when touched because an electric signal runs through the leaf. A bumblebee senses the faint electricity around a flower.

teachings.teaching: In the teaching called the honey knowledge, the sage says that lightning is like honey for all beings, and all beings are like honey for lightning. The shining one in the lightning and the shining one inside a person are one and the same.
teachings.link: Science finds that the force in lightning and the force in our nerves are the same electric force. The Upanishad saw a likeness between the light in the sky and the light inside us.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says that a person who does not guard against harm before it comes will be destroyed, like a heap of straw before a fire.
teachings.link: Electrical safety is guarding before harm comes. You dry your hands before the switch, not after the shock.

science.text: Nerves carry messages as tiny electric signals, made by salts moving in and out of nerve cells. A heart's beat is set off by electric signals, which an ECG machine can read.
Plants send electric signals too. When a touch-me-not is touched, an electric signal runs through the leaf, and the leaflets fold. Bumblebees can sense the faint electricity around flowers.

other_view.view: Lightning, the wall socket and a nerve all use electric charge, but that is a fact of physics, not a sign that they are one being. A nerve signal is made by a living cell, and lightning is made by charge moving through air. Calling them the same, they say, hides how different they are.

practice.title: The dry-hands pause
practice.say: Stand in front of the switch board. Do not touch it yet. Look at your hands. Turn them over slowly. Breathe in and out once. Now rub them on the towel, front and back, counting to ten. Feel how warm and dry they are. Then press the switch. Do this every time, and drying your hands becomes a habit.
practice.kid: Stand by the switch. Look at your hands. Breathe once. Dry them on the towel. Count to ten. Then press the switch.

science: Mains supply in India: 230 volts, 50 hertz (Bureau of Indian Standards, IS 12360). Common torch cells: 1.5 volts.

Skin resistance falls sharply when skin is wet: dry skin can be around 100,000 ohms, wet skin around 1,000 ohms (widely cited in electrical safety guidance, for example the US Occupational Safety and Health Administration).

Stephen Gray, 'A Letter... containing several Experiments concerning Electricity', Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, 1731: the long packthread on silk supports (1729, with Granvile Wheler) and the boy suspended on silk cords (1730). Gray received the first Copley Medal in 1731.

A. Lalitha (1919 to 1979): studied electrical engineering at the College of Engineering, Guindy, graduating in the 1940s, among India's first women engineers. She later worked with Associated Electrical Industries on equipment for the Bhakra Nangal project.
Clarke D, Whitney H, Sutton G, Robert D, Detection and learning of floral electric fields by bumblebees, Science, 2013.
Touch-me-not (Mimosa pudica) leaf folding is set off by electrical signals (action potentials) travelling through the leaf (studied since J.C. Bose and others).
De Santana CD and others, Unexpected species diversity in electric eels, Nature Communications, 2019: Electrophorus voltai discharges up to about 860 volts.
Residual current devices (RCCB) trip within about 0.3 seconds at their rated leakage current, and faster at higher leakage (IS 12640).
Debate on plug-in socket covers: UK safety campaigners and the Institution of Engineering and Technology have said covers are not needed for UK shuttered sockets and some can defeat the shutters.
